title: She didn’t come for curiosity. That’s what most people get wrong.
paragraphs: She didn’t come for curiosity. That’s what most people get wrong.

When the Queen of Sheba set out to see Solomon, it wasn’t tourism, diplomacy, or spectacle. It was a search. A restless, internal pulling that no wealth, no throne, no power could quiet. Scripture says, “When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the Lord, she came to test him with hard questions” (1 Kings 10:1). Read that again. His fame was tied to the name of the Lord.
That changes everything.
Because what drew her wasn’t merely a wise king. It was the evidence of a God she had not yet encountered.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

Imagine the journey. Long, exhausting, deliberate. Caravans heavy with gold, spices, and precious stones. Not because she needed to impress Solomon—but because she understood something about value. You don’t approach what is sacred casually. You don’t come empty when your soul is hungry for truth.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
She wasn’t just testing Solomon.
God was exposing her.

You can almost feel the tension when she arrives. The questions weren’t shallow. They were the kind that keep you awake at night. The kind you don’t say out loud because they reveal too much. Questions about meaning. About power. About what lasts when everything else fades.
And Solomon answered all her questions. Scripture says nothing was hidden from him.
Nothing.
That’s unsettling, isn’t it?

Because you’ve done the same thing. You’ve rehearsed questions in your mind. You’ve searched for answers in success, relationships, distractions. You’ve tried to outthink the emptiness. But deep down…
You knew.
There was something missing.
The Queen of Sheba walked into a kingdom where wisdom wasn’t just spoken—it was visible. The order. The abundance. The servants. The structure. The peace. It reflected something beyond human effort.
It reflected God.
“And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon’s wisdom… there was no more spirit in her” (1 Kings 10:4-5).
She was undone.
Not impressed.
Undone.
Because true wisdom doesn’t entertain you. It confronts you.
God saw it.
She came with pride, position, and questions. But standing in the evidence of God’s blessing, she realized something devastating.
Everything she had built without God was incomplete.
That’s the turning point most people avoid.
You’ll admire truth. You’ll listen to sermons. You’ll even acknowledge wisdom. But surrender?
That’s where resistance rises.
The Queen of Sheba didn’t resist.
She confessed.
“Blessed be the Lord your God, who delighted in you… because the Lord loved Israel forever” (1 Kings 10:9).
She recognized the source.
Not Solomon.
God.
This is where the meaning deepens beyond history.
Because Solomon, in all his wisdom, was only a shadow.

Jesus Christ said, “The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment… for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42).
Something greater.
You’re not just reading about a queen visiting a king.
You’re being confronted with a choice.
She traveled miles to hear truth.
You have it in front of you—and still hesitate.
Why?
Because acknowledging wisdom is easy.
Repenting is not.
The Queen of Sheba’s journey exposes a deeper reality: when truth is revealed, neutrality is no longer an option. You either humble yourself before God, or you walk away unchanged.
There is no middle ground.
And here’s the part that should shake you.
She responded with awe, humility, and giving. She didn’t leave the same. The encounter produced transformation.
But many today encounter something far greater—Jesus Christ Himself—and remain untouched.
That’s not lack of evidence.
That’s resistance of the heart.
Jesus is not just wisdom. He is the embodiment of truth. “In Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). And unlike Solomon, He didn’t just answer questions.
He dealt with sin.
Directly.
You’ve asked questions about purpose, pain, direction. But beneath all of that is the real issue.
Sin separates.
And until that is confronted, no answer will satisfy.
The Queen of Sheba saw glory and responded.
You’ve seen the cross.

You’ve heard that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). You’ve heard that “the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23).
You’ve heard it.
But have you responded?
Because the meaning behind her visit isn’t admiration.
It’s revelation leading to surrender.
She didn’t just acknowledge greatness.
She honored it.
So here you are.
You’ve seen enough. You’ve heard enough. The question isn’t whether truth is available.
The question is whether you will bow to it.
Say it plainly if you feel it rising in you: I can’t stay the same.
Follow this journey if you’re ready for truth that doesn’t bend.
